title: Watch It or Push It: Reporters and Actuators

scenes.visual: Deep navy canvas (#0B132B). One living neuron outline in ice-blue (#89CFF0) fills 65% of the frame height, with faint ambient drift particles. Title fades in clean white (size 44): 'Watch It or Push It: Reporters and Actuators', then clears cleanly while the neuron stays anchored.

scenes.tts: Every time a mouse turns left, one hidden neuron fires. How can you watch that living signal, and test whether it causes the turn? Signals inside cells are tiny and fast. Engineered proteins let you answer both questions with light.
scenes.caption: Every time a mouse turns left, one hidden neuron fires. How can you watch that living signal, and test whether it causes the turn? Signals inside cells are tiny and fast. Engineered proteins let you answer both questions with light.
scenes.visual: Carry the ice-blue neuron (#89CFF0). Top-left schematic mouse silhouette turns left; a faint golden pulse (#FACC15) ripples down the neuron while tiny amber calcium dots (#F4A261) drift inside. A soft question badge 'Watch? Test cause?' fades in beside the neuron as the pulse repeats.
scenes.narration: Every time a mouse turns left, one hidden neuron fires. How can you watch that living signal, and test whether it causes the turn? Signals inside cells are tiny and fast. Engineered proteins let you answer both questions with light.

scenes.tts: Two kinds of protein do the work. A reporter turns a cell's signal into light so you can watch it live. An actuator works the other way. It turns a flash of light or a drug into a signal on command.
scenes.caption: Two kinds of protein do the work. A reporter turns a cell's signal into light so you can watch it live. An actuator works the other way. It turns a flash of light or a drug into a signal on command.
scenes.visual: Keep the same neuron centered. On its left dendrite, an emerald arrow (#2ECC71) points outward from an amber calcium dot to a glowing light ray labeled 'Reporter: signal to light'. On its right membrane, a sky-blue beam (#38BDF8) points inward to a coral pore (#FB7185) labeled 'Actuator: command to signal'. Both labels size 30.
scenes.narration: Two kinds of protein do the work. A reporter turns a cell's signal into light so you can watch it live. An actuator works the other way. It turns a flash of light or a drug into a signal on command.

scenes.tts: Reporters start with green fluorescent protein from a jellyfish. How does fluorescence work? A molecule absorbs a blue photon and lifts an electron. A little energy leaves as heat before a green photon comes out. So light leaves at a longer wavelength than it entered.
scenes.caption: Reporters start with green fluorescent protein from a jellyfish. How does fluorescence work? A molecule absorbs a blue photon and lifts an electron. A little energy leaves as heat before a green photon comes out. So light leaves at a longer wavelength than it entered.
scenes.visual: Zoom smoothly inside the neuron's cytosol to a simple cartoon emerald barrel (#2ECC71, no molecular structure) with a glowing central dot. A schematic energy ladder appears beside it: a sky-blue wave (#38BDF8, labeled 'Blue in') lifts an electron dot up, a tiny wavy red arrow ('Heat lost') drops it slightly, and an emerald wave ('Green out') exits downward.
scenes.narration: Reporters start with green fluorescent protein from a jellyfish. How does fluorescence work? A molecule absorbs a blue photon and lifts an electron. A little energy leaves as heat before a green photon comes out. So light leaves at a longer wavelength than it entered.

scenes.tts: Green fluorescent protein folds into a tight barrel with its glowing center shielded inside. Under blue light, that sealed barrel glows steadily. To make brightness track calcium, engineers cut a narrow slit beside that glowing center. Water slips through the slit and dims the glow.
scenes.caption: Green fluorescent protein folds into a tight barrel with its glowing center shielded inside. Under blue light, that sealed barrel glows steadily. To make brightness track calcium, engineers cut a narrow slit beside that glowing center. Water slips through the slit and dims the glow.
scenes.visual: Transform the same emerald barrel in place (65% frame height). First it glows steadily with pale-cyan water droplets (#BAE6FD) bouncing harmlessly off its sealed wall. Then scissors-free clean split opens a narrow gap in the side wall; water droplets drift into the gap and the emerald glow dims to faint olive.
scenes.narration: Green fluorescent protein folds into a tight barrel with its glowing center shielded inside. Under blue light, that sealed barrel glows steadily. To make brightness track calcium, engineers cut a narrow slit beside that glowing center. Water slips through the slit and dims the glow.

scenes.tts: Next, engineers attach a calcium detector called calmodulin to one edge, and a partner peptide to the other. That hybrid sensor is G camp. When calcium enters, calmodulin grabs it and wraps around the peptide. Together they plug the slit, shut water out, and brighten the barrel.
scenes.caption: Next, engineers attach a calcium detector called calmodulin to one edge, and a partner peptide to the other. That hybrid sensor is GCaMP. When calcium enters, calmodulin grabs it and wraps around the peptide. Together they plug the slit, shut water out, and brighten the barrel.
scenes.visual: Keep the slit barrel in place. Attach a teal crescent ('Calmodulin') to one lip of the slit and a short white bar ('Peptide') to the other; label the assembly 'GCaMP'. Amber calcium spheres (#F4A261) stream in and bind calmodulin, which smoothly wraps around the peptide to seal the gap; pale-cyan water retreats and the emerald barrel flares bright.
scenes.narration: Next, engineers attach a calcium detector called calmodulin to one edge, and a partner peptide to the other. That hybrid sensor is GCaMP. When calcium enters, calmodulin grabs it and wraps around the peptide. Together they plug the slit, shut water out, and brighten the barrel.

scenes.tts: Every time the mouse turns left, this G camp neuron flashes bright green. Pause and think. Does that flash prove firing this neuron causes the turn, or could another circuit drive both?
scenes.caption: Every time the mouse turns left, this GCaMP neuron flashes bright green. Pause and think. Does that flash prove firing this neuron causes the turn, or could another circuit drive both?
scenes.visual: Zoom out smoothly to the full ice-blue neuron inside the schematic brain silhouette while the mouse icon turns left. Each turn triggers an emerald flash inside the neuron and a rising schematic green trace labeled 'GCaMP light (schematic)'. A clean question card slides in at top: 'Does the flash prove causation?'
scenes.narration: Every time the mouse turns left, this GCaMP neuron flashes bright green. Pause and think. Does that flash prove firing this neuron causes the turn, or could another circuit drive both?

scenes.visual: Hold the question card 'Does the flash prove causation?' above the softly pulsing emerald neuron and schematic mouse icon. Slow drifting ambient dots and a gentle progress bar along the bottom edge mark the 4.5-second thinking pause.

scenes.tts: Watching alone cannot prove causation, because another brain circuit could drive both the turn and the calcium flash at once. So to test causation, you cannot only watch. You must push this neuron yourself and see what the mouse does.
scenes.caption: Watching alone cannot prove causation, because another brain circuit could drive both the turn and the calcium flash at once. So to test causation, you cannot only watch. You must push this neuron yourself and see what the mouse does.
scenes.visual: From above the neuron, a muted slate upstream box labeled 'Other circuit?' fades in with two dashed arrows—one to the mouse turning left, one to the glowing neuron—illustrating shared drive. Then that upstream box dims as a sky-blue light beam icon appears beside the neuron's membrane.
scenes.narration: Watching alone cannot prove causation, because another brain circuit could drive both the turn and the calcium flash at once. So to test causation, you cannot only watch. You must push this neuron yourself and see what the mouse does.

scenes.tts: That takes an actuator. Meet channelrhodopsin two, borrowed from a green alga. Like rhodopsin in your eye, it holds light-sensing retinal inside seven membrane helices. Your eye's protein then passes the message to a G protein, a go-between. Channelrhodopsin two skips that go-between: it is itself an ion pore.
scenes.caption: That takes an actuator. Meet channelrhodopsin-2, borrowed from a green alga. Like rhodopsin in your eye, it holds light-sensing retinal inside seven membrane helices. Your eye's protein then passes the message to a G protein, a go-between. Channelrhodopsin-2 skips that go-between: it is itself an ion pore.
scenes.visual: Pan smoothly to a cross-section of the same ice-blue neuron's membrane. Insert a coral-orange seven-cylinder cartoon ('Channelrhodopsin-2') with a bright gold bar inside ('Retinal'). Briefly ghost a side-by-side 'Eye rhodopsin -> G protein' arrow that fades away with a soft dash, leaving only the coral channel's central closed pore.
scenes.narration: That takes an actuator. Meet channelrhodopsin-2, borrowed from a green alga. Like rhodopsin in your eye, it holds light-sensing retinal inside seven membrane helices. Your eye's protein then passes the message to a G protein, a go-between. Channelrhodopsin-2 skips that go-between: it is itself an ion pore.

scenes.tts: Flash blue light onto the membrane. Retinal shifts shape, and the pore opens within milliseconds. Cations rush in, and their positive charge makes the inside less negative. The voltage climbs past the firing threshold, the neuron fires, and the mouse turns left.
scenes.caption: Flash blue light onto the membrane. Retinal shifts shape, and the pore opens within milliseconds. Cations rush in, and their positive charge makes the inside less negative. The voltage climbs past the firing threshold, the neuron fires, and the mouse turns left.
scenes.visual: A vivid sky-blue beam (#38BDF8) hits the coral channel. The gold retinal bar bends, the coral cylinders swing apart, and bright amber/white '+' spheres stream inward. Below, a warm gold curve ('Voltage, schematic') rises past a dashed 'Threshold' line into a sharp spike, lighting the neuron and turning the schematic mouse left.
scenes.narration: Flash blue light onto the membrane. Retinal shifts shape, and the pore opens within milliseconds. Cations rush in, and their positive charge makes the inside less negative. The voltage climbs past the firing threshold, the neuron fires, and the mouse turns left.

scenes.tts: Both tools are engineered proteins that living cells can build from a gene. Put them together and you hold the first rule. Reporters turn signals into light, and actuators control them on command.
scenes.caption: Both tools are engineered proteins that living cells can build from a gene. Put them together and you hold the first rule. Reporters turn signals into light, and actuators control them on command.
scenes.visual: Zoom out slightly so the single ice-blue neuron carries both the emerald GCaMP barrel pulsing with calcium on the left and the coral channelrhodopsin-2 pore opening to a sky-blue pulse on the right, both continuously active in calm motion.
scenes.narration: Both tools are engineered proteins that living cells can build from a gene. Put them together and you hold the first rule. Reporters turn signals into light, and actuators control them on command.
